Citation: CL v Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2025 SST 174
Social Security Tribunal of Canada Appeal Division
Leave to Appeal Decision
Applicant: C. L.
Respondent: Canada Employment Insurance Commission
Decision under appeal: General Division decision dated January 31, 2025
(GE-24-4046)
Tribunal member: Glenn Betteridge
Decision date: February 27, 2025
File number: AD-25-121
On this page
Decision Overview Issue I’m not giving the Claimant permission to appeal Conclusion
Decision [1] Leave (permission) to appeal is refused. The appeal won’t go forward.
Overview [2] C. L. is the Claimant. Her employer terminated her employment. Then she made a claim for Employment Insurance (EI) regular benefits.
[3] This Tribunal’s General Division dismissed her appeal. It found her employer dismissed her because she didn’t comply with its requirement to return to work full-time in the office, during regular business hours. And it found that reason counted as misconduct under the Employment Insurance Act (EI Act). So the Commission disqualified her from getting benefits.
[4] The Claimant wants to appeal the General Division decision. She says the General Division made an important factual error. It ignored her safety and security concerns. She worked at a Jewish organization post-October 7, 2023. There had been threats and incidents. She says the General Division’s lack of regard for her concerns is anti-Semitic.
[5] I can give the Claimant permission to appeal if she shows her appeal has a reasonable chance of success. Unfortunately, she hasn’t.
Issue [6] Does the Claimant’s appeal have a reasonable chance of success?
I’m not giving the Claimant permission to appeal [7] I appreciate the Claimant had valid concerns for her personal safety at work. She also faced changes at work. She was a long-time employee reporting to a new executive director. And the board was involved in day-to-day operations like never before.
[8] How she acted on her concerns and responded to the changes caused her employer to dismiss her. She didn’t want to work from the office full-time. She refused when her employer told her she had to. She says her employer seemed unwilling to compromise on remote (hybrid) work and did nothing to address her safety concerns.
[9] She says she asked her employer for a severance package because she felt bullied and “boxed in.” Her employer prepared a severance package and dismissed her.
[10] The relevant evidence shows the Claimant caused her unemployment. It wasn’t involuntary. So, the General Division decided she was disqualified from getting benefits (paragraphs 2, and 32 to 36). But there isn’t an arguable case the General Division made an error that gives her appeal a reasonable chance of success.
[11] For these reasons and the reasons that follow, I am not giving the Claimant permission to appeal.
The permission to appeal test screens out appeals with no reasonable chance of successFootnote 1 [12] I can give the Claimant permission to appeal if her appeal has a reasonable chance of success.Footnote 2 This means she has to show an arguable ground of appeal upon which her appeal might succeed.Footnote 3
[13] The law lets me consider four grounds of appeal, which I will call errors. The General DivisionFootnote 4
used an unfair process or was biased (a procedural fairness error) didn’t use its decision-making power properly (a jurisdictional error) made a legal error made an important factual error
[14] I will start by considering the Claimant’s reasons for appeal.Footnote 5 These reasons set out the key issues and central arguments I have to consider.Footnote 6 The Claimant is representing herself. So I will also consider whether the General Division might have made other errors she didn’t identify.Footnote 7
There isn’t an arguable case the General Division made an important factual error, and it used the correct legal test for misconduct [15] The Claimant checked the box that says the General Division made an important error of fact.
[16] The General Division makes an important factual error if it bases its decision on a factual finding it made by ignoring or misunderstanding relevant evidence.Footnote 8 Relevant means legally relevant.
[17] The Claimant argues the General Division didn’t seem to understand the point of her claim. She refused to work in the office full-time because her employer didn’t have armed security to protect staff against anti-Semitic attacks. She says, “The employer did nothing to place additional security measures to deal with this nor demonstrated any understanding of my concern.”Footnote 9
[18] I can’t accept the Claimant’s argument. It misunderstands the legal test for misconduct and the evidence that’s relevant to that test.
Misconduct focuses on the employee’s conduct and their entitlement to benefits, not the employer’s conduct [19] The Federal Court of Appeal recently explained the law about misconduct like this:
The Employment Insurance Act governs the relationship between the unemployed person and any entitlement to benefits, not the employee’s contract of employment. […]The Act itself does not define misconduct – that has been left to the Social Security Tribunal and this Court, which has held that misconduct occurs where an employee chooses to engage in conduct which would impair the performance of their duties… Consequently, the only question is whether the employee was aware or ought to have been aware of the employer’s policy, the consequences of failing to comply with that policy and engaged in conduct which, objectively, could lead to a loss of employment. Questions such as whether the dismissal was unfair or unjust, whether the policy was well founded, whether there were options short of dismissal and whether the policy or dismissal conformed to the collective agreement are irrelevant to the inquiry as to whether the claimant is entitled to benefits.Footnote 10 [Emphasis added.]
[20] In that appeal, the claimant breached the employer’s policy. In this appeal, the Claimant breached the employer’s direction to return to work full-time in the office. But this makes no difference to the legal test.
[21] The General Division set out the correct legal test for misconduct (paragraphs 10, 11, 17 to 20). It cited court decisions it had to follow (paragraphs 28 to 32, 35 and 36). Then it used that test and those decisions to decide the Claimant’s appeal (paragraphs 21 to 34).
[22] The General Division could not base its decision on the employer’s conduct. So evidence of what her employer did or failed to do—and the Claimant’s assessment of office safety—wasn’t relevant. The General Division had to decide whether the Claimant’s conduct counted as misconduct under the EI Act. And it did exactly that.
[23] The Astolfi decision says there are appeals when General Division should consider whether the employer’s prior conduct caused the employee’s alleged misconduct.Footnote 11 If it did, the employee’s conduct isn’t wilful (conscious, deliberate, or intentional) and doesn’t count as misconduct.
[24] This isn’t one of those appeals. The evidence doesn’t show the Claimant refused to work in the office after her employer harassed or threatened her.Footnote 12
[25] The Claimant testified she thought the board president was a bully in the way she made decisions. She didn’t consult or listen to staff. So the Claimant complained to the board’s HR committee. When the Claimant and her employer disagreed at the in-person meeting in June, her employer kept repeating it would have to “go to legal.” She explained this made her feel “boxed in,” like her employer was forcing her to quit—that’s why she asked for a severance package.Footnote 13
[26] But she asked for a severance package via email, the day before the meeting (paragraph 33).Footnote 14 And she refused to work from the office full-time because she says she knew better than her employer when she needed to be in the office to do her job (paragraph 26).
[27] So, the General Division didn’t need to consider the Astolfi decision. It considered the relevant evidence—including the timing of events—and concluded the Claimant’s conduct was wilful (paragraphs 21, 26, and 33).
The relevant evidence and the purpose of EI benefits support the General Division decision [28] The relevant evidence shows the Claimant disagreed with her employer about the terms and conditions of her work. They disagreed about the threat level and the adequacy of the employer’s security measures.Footnote 15 They disagreed about in-office versus hybrid work and whether she needed to be in the office to do her job.
[29] In response to these disagreements, the Claimant made the deliberate decision not to comply with her employer’s requirement to return to work full-time in the office (paragraphs 22 and 29). And her employer dismissed her because of that (paragraph 15).
[30] So there isn’t an arguable case the General Division made an important factual error when it discounted the Claimant’s evidence that her employer didn’t make her workplace safe. That evidence wasn’t legally relevant.
[31] And the General Division didn’t have to accept her argument about the point of her claim. That argument goes against the law about misconduct.
[32] The General Division’s decision is supported by the relevant evidence and follows the purpose of EI benefits.
[33] I reviewed the documents before the General Division, listened to the hearing, and read its decision. The General Division didn’t ignore or misunderstand any relevant evidence. The relevant evidence supports the decision.
[34] The courts have said benefits are for people who are involuntarily unemployed. In other words, people who cause their unemployment can’t get benefits. Unfortunately for the Claimant, this is what she did. The General Division decided that she caused her unemployment when she deliberately refused to go into the office and asked for a severance package (paragraphs 13, 21, 22, 29, and 33).
[35] The courts have said a claimant can use other legal avenues to challenge their employer’s conduct. For example, an employee can sue for wrongful dismissal, file a human rights complaint, or make a complaint under health and safety law. The General Division made this point (paragraph 35).
There isn’t an arguable case the General Division member was prejudiced or used an unfair process [36] The Claimant says the General Division member was biased or prejudiced against her.
[37] She argues the “individuals reviewing this case” were anti-Semitic. She says they demonstrated a lack of knowledge of the environment and anti-Semitic behaviour by not understanding the point of her claim. She is referring to the climate of anti-Semitism across Canada and the world, including anti-Semitic incidents, after October 7, 2023. She says this made her workplace unsafe for her.
[38] The legal test to show a tribunal member was biased or prejudged the case is difficult to meet.Footnote 16 A tribunal member is presumed to be impartial. The person who alleges bias has to show a reasonably informed person would think, in the circumstances, the decision-maker would not decide fairly.Footnote 17
[39] The Claimant didn’t refer to any anti-Semitic conduct during the hearing or anti-Semitic statements in the General Division decision.
[40] I read the General Division decision and listened to the General Division hearing recording. I didn’t read or hear anything that would suggest to a reasonably informed person the member was anti-Semitic or otherwise biased or prejudiced against the Claimant.
[41] The General Division didn’t accept her argument that her conduct wasn’t wilful because her employer didn’t take her security concerns seriously. But this doesn’t show the member was anti-Semitic. As I explained above, the member could not accept her argument. It goes against the law of misconduct. And this meant her evidence about what her employer did or failed to do (take her concerns seriously and hire armed security) wasn’t relevant.
[42] So, the Claimant hasn’t shown there is an arguable case the General Division member prejudged her appeal or was biased against her. And I didn’t find an arguable case.
[43] The General Division gave the Claimant an opportunity to know the case she had to meet.
[44] At the hearing, the Claimant said she received and had reviewed the Commission’s evidence (GD3) and written arguments (GD4). The General Division explained the law and let her present her case. Then it asked her to respond to questions raised by the Commission’s evidence and arguments. And her witness testified. Finally, the General Division gave the Claimant the chance to say anything else she hadn’t already said.
[45] This shows me the General Division gave her a full and fair opportunity to present her case.
[46] So there isn’t an arguable case the General Division process was unfair to the Claimant.
Conclusion [47] The Claimant hasn’t shown an arguable case the General Division made an error that might allow her appeal to succeed. And I didn’t find an arguable case.
[48] This means her appeal doesn’t have a reasonable chance of success. So I can’t give her permission to appeal the General Division decision.
